note.text: Systems differ in who owns productive resources and how decisions are coordinated. Private ownership places assets under individuals or firms. Public ownership places assets under the state or a public body. Markets coordinate many decisions through exchange and prices; planning coordinates through deliberate decisions and instructions. Traditional arrangements may rely on custom. Actual economies combine institutions, so a single private shop or state project cannot by itself classify an entire national economy.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Systems differ in who owns productive resources and how decisions are coordinated. Private ownership places assets under individuals or firms. Public ownership places assets under the state or a public body. Markets coordinate many decisions through exchange and prices; planning coordinates through deliberate decisions and instructions. Traditional arrangements may rely on custom. Actual economies combine institutions, so a single private shop or state project cannot by itself classify an entire national economy.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A family stall in Bamenda may be privately owned, while a public service belongs to a state body. A school can plan its timetable even within a wider market economy. Distinguish the institution being described from the whole country's system. Classification should use ownership and coordination together, rather than whether money appears in the story.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask who controls the resource, who makes the decision and what coordinates other decisions. Do not assume public ownership means nobody is responsible, or private ownership means no rules apply. Use mixed arrangements when the evidence shows more than one mechanism.
